label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claim: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.
quote: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.
scope: growing multicellular plant and animal structures

label: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm
claim: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
quote: for the actual _precipitation_ takes place, as a rule, not in actively living, but in dead or at least inactive tissue: that is to say in the “formed material” or matrix which (as for instance in cartilage) accumulates round the living cells
scope: calcified and silicified skeletal elements of animals and plants (spicules, concretions, cartilage and bone)

label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claim: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
quote: the eggs of sea-urchins reared in lime-free water develop in apparent health, into larvae entirely destitute of the usual skeleton of calcareous rods, and in which, accordingly, the long arms of the Pluteus larva, which the rods support and distend, are entirely suppressed.
scope: echinoid pluteus larvae (and by extension skeleton-forming organisms deprived of skeletal material)

label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight
claim: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
quote: an example limited but yet crucial (_if confirmed_), of an asymmetric force, non-vital in its origin, which might conceivably be the starting-point of that asymmetry which is characteristic of so many organic products.
scope: optically active (chiral) compounds produced by living organisms; origin of biological homochirality

label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites
claim: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
quote: The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
scope: pearls, molluscan and teleost otoliths, and similar calcareous concretions

label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claim: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
quote: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.
scope: fish scales and otoliths, bones, starch grains and other concentrically zoned organic structures

label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claim: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
quote: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.
section: Solubility of calcium salts in colloids
scope: calcified tissues of animals, especially bone and calcareous skeletons

label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
claim: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
quote: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.
section: Classification of skeletal forms by scale
scope: skeletal elements of all sizes, from protist skeletons and spicules to vertebrate bones

label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic
claim: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
quote: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.
section: Spicules confined to a cell surface
scope: small curved intracellular spicules of sponges and holothurians (sigmata, amphidiscs and similar)

label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry
claim: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
quote: the Holothurian spicules are composed of calcium carbonate while those which we have just described in the case of sponges are usually, if not always, siliceous: this being just another proof of the fact that in such cases the form of the spicule is not due to its chemical nature or molecular structure, but to the external forces
section: Spicules confined to a cell surface
scope: sponge and holothurian spicules

label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claim: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
quote: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°
scope: triradiate and tetractinellid spicules of calcareous and tetractinellid sponges

label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles
claim: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
quote: the cells or vesicles by which they are conformed are not arranged in what is known as “closest packing,” but in linear series; so that in their arrangement, and by their mutual compression, we tend to get a pattern, not of hexagons, but of squares: or, looking to the solid, not of dodecahedra but of cubes or parallelopipeda.
scope: hexactinellid (glass) sponges

label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claim: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
quote: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat
scope: Radiolaria, living and fossil

label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill
claim: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
quote: The formation of an “agglutinated” shell is thus seen to be a purely physical phenomenon, and indeed a special case of a more general physical phenomenon which has many other important consequences in biology.
scope: agglutinated testate amoebae and foraminifera

label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
claim: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
quote: it will at once follow that they will show a tendency to aggregate in the grooves which separate the vesicles, and the result will be the development of a most delicate sphere composed of tiny rods arranged in a regular hexagonal network
scope: spherical lattice-shelled Radiolaria (e.g. Aulonia, Actinomma, Cenosphaera)

label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles
claim: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
quote: This is only another proof (if proof be needed) that the peculiar conformation of these little skeletons is not due to the material of which they are composed, but to the moulding of that material upon an underlying vesicular structure.
scope: Radiolaria and Heliozoa with lattice skeletons of different composition

label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells
claim: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
quote: It is obvious at a glance that this is such a skeleton as may have been formed (I think we may go so far as to say _must_ have been formed) at the interfaces of a little tetrahedral group of cells
scope: Nassellaria with tetrahedral skeletons (e.g. Callimitra)

label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning
claim: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
quote: If we may safely judge from Haeckel’s figures, the pentagonal dodecahedron of the Radiolarian is perfectly regular, and we must presume, accordingly, that it is not brought about by principles of space-partitioning similar to those which manifest themselves in the phenomenon of crystallisation.
scope: polyhedral Radiolaria (Circoporidae and allies)

label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claim: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
quote: The true symmetry of this figure, then, is hexagonal, with a polar axis, produced into two polar spicules; with six equatorial spicules, or rays; and with two sets of six spicular rays, interposed between the polar axis and the equatorial rays, and alternating in position with the latter.
scope: Acantharia and allied Radiolaria with twenty radial spines (e.g. Dorataspis, Phatnaspis)

label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics
claim: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
quote: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism
scope: Radiolaria with fixed numbers and positions of radial spines (Acantharia, Phaeodaria)

label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics
claim: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.
quote: These three systems are all of frequent occurrence, and are all illustrated in the local thickenings of the wall of the cylindrical cells or vessels of plants.
scope: plant xylem vessels and tracheids, insect tracheae

label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
claim: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
quote: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella
scope: high-spired gastropod shells (e.g. Turritella)

label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns
claim: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
quote: and it is also common to find the two systems interfering with one another, and forming a criss-cross, or reticulated arrangement. This is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
scope: reticulated patterns on cylindrical and curved organic surfaces (cell walls, integuments)

label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves
claim: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
quote: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow
scope: muscular walls of hollow and tubular organs (heart, stomach, blood vessels, gut, worm body wall)

label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube
claim: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
quote: these systems of muscular fibres, geodetic to begin with, remain geodetic (in the sense in which we are using the word) after all the twisting to which the primitive cylindrical tube or tubes have been subjected.
scope: vertebrate (especially mammalian) heart and stomach musculature

label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claim: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
quote: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.
scope: ciliates, flagellates, rotifers, swarm-spores and other small swimming organisms

label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
claim: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
quote: Of the spiral forms which we have now mentioned, every one (with the single exception of the outline of the cordate leaf) is an example of the remarkable curve known as the Logarithmic Spiral.
scope: ruminant horns, molluscan shells, foraminiferal shells, sunflower capitula; excludes cordate leaf outlines

label: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one
claim: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.
quote: the growing curve will tend to wind round and round its point of origin. In the typical case of the snail-shell, such an intrinsic force is manifestly present in the action of the columellar muscle.
scope: spirally growing shells and other growing structures subject to deflecting forces

label: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral
claim: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.
quote: In other words, in such a structure as we have presupposed, the existence or maintenance of a constant ratio between the rates of extension or growth in the vertical and transverse directions will lead, in general, to the development of a logarithmic spiral; the magnitude of that ratio will determine the character (that is to say, the constant angle) of the spiral;
scope: tubular shells and horns growing by unequal accretion

label: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral
claim: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.
quote: The result is that the successive shoots, or successive increments of growth, are tangents to a curve, and this curve is a true logarithmic spiral.
scope: scorpioid and helicoid (cymose) inflorescences, e.g. borage

label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape
claim: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.
quote: The shell, like the creature within it, grows in size _but does not change its shape_; and the existence of this constant relativity of growth, or constant similarity of form, is of the essence, and may be made the basis of a definition, of the logarithmic spiral.
scope: molluscan shells, horns and other structures growing by terminal accretion

label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
claim: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.
quote: (2) it is characteristic of the growth of the horn, of the shell, and of all other organic forms in which a logarithmic spiral can be recognised, that _each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the entire pre-existing structure_.
scope: molluscan shells and opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns, tusks

label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts
claim: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.
quote: For it follows as a simple corollary to this theorem of gnomons that we must not expect to find the logarithmic spiral manifested in a structure whose parts are simultaneously produced, as for instance in the margin of a leaf, or among the many curves that make the contour of a fish.
scope: organic curves in general; accretionary hard parts versus soft tissues and leaf margins

label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
claim: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
quote: It was by observing, with the help of very careful measurement, this continued proportionality, that Moseley was enabled to verify his first assumption, based on the general appearance of the shell, that the shell of Nautilus was actually a logarithmic spiral, and this demonstration he was immediately afterwards in a position to generalise by extending it to all the spiral Ammonitoid and Gastropod mollusca
section: Measuring the spiral of the shell
scope: Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropod shells

label: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios
claim: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.
quote: In short it is obvious that _all_ the differences of form which we observe between one shell and another are referable to matters of _degree_, depending, one and all, upon the relative magnitudes of the various factors in the complex equation to the curve.
scope: univalve (discoid and turbinate) molluscan shells

label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
claim: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
quote: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.
scope: Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropods

label: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border
claim: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.
quote: For the purposes of the morphologist, then, the main result of this last general investigation is to shew that all the various types of “open” and “closed” spirals, all the various degrees of separation or overlap of the successive whorls, are simply the outward expression of a varying ratio in the _rate of growth_ of the outer as compared with the inner border of the tubular shell.
scope: discoid and turbinate molluscan shells, including nautiloids and ammonoids

label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry
claim: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.
quote: _To such phylogenetic hypotheses the mathematical or dynamical study of the forms of shells lends no valid support._ If we have two shells in which the constant angle of the spire be respectively 80° and 60°, that fact in itself does not at all justify an assertion that the one is more primitive, more ancient, or more “ancestral” than the other.
scope: cephalopod (nautiloid and ammonoid) shell forms and phylogenetic inference from them

label: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence
claim: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.
quote: And to my mind, the mathematical (as distinguished from the purely physical) study of morphology bids fair to help us to recognise this phenomenon of orthogenesis in many cases where it is not at once patent to the eye; and also, on the other hand, to warn us, in many other cases, that even strong and apparently complex resemblances in form may be capable of arising independently,
scope: fossil and living lineages, especially molluscan shells

label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites
claim: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).
quote: But let us suppose that the spiral angle increases somewhat rapidly; we shall then get a spiral with gradually narrowing whorls, and this condition is characteristic of Oekotraustes, a subgenus of Ammonites. If on the other hand, the angle α gradually diminishes, and even falls away to zero, we shall have the spiral curve opening out, as it does in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites,
section: Changes of spiral angle with age
scope: ammonoids and nautiloids with changing coiling (e.g. Oekotraustes, Scaphites, Ancyloceras, Lituites)

label: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle
claim: Shells as different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little in their spiral angle (the ratio of radial to tangential growth) and differ in form mainly in the apical angle of the enveloping cone, which is set by the rate of translation along the axis relative to growth.
quote: We see from this that shells so different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little indeed in the magnitude of the spiral angle α, that is to say in the relative velocities of radial and tangential growth. It is upon the angle θ that the difference in their form mainly depends:
scope: turbinate and discoid gastropod shells

label: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate
claim: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).
quote: All that we are immediately concerned with is the simple fact that where a velocity, such as our rate of growth, varies with its direction,—varies that is to say as a function of the angular divergence from a certain axis,—then, in a certain simple case, we get lines of growth laid down as a system of coaxial circles,
scope: lamellibranch and brachiopod shells with visible growth lines

label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines
claim: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.
quote: But in Estheria (and one or two other small crustacea) the moult is incomplete: the old carapace is retained, and the new, growing up underneath it, adheres to it like a lining, and projects beyond its edge: so that in course of time the margins of successive old carapaces appear as “lines of growth” upon the surface of the shell.
scope: Estheria and similar conchostracan crustaceans

label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint
claim: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.
quote: It is obvious that the incipient curvature of the arms, and consequently the form and direction of the spirals, will be influenced by the surrounding pressures, and these in turn by the general shape of the shell. We shall expect, accordingly, to find the long outwardly directed spirals associated with shells which are transversely elongated, as Spirifer is; while the more rounded Atrypas will tend to the opposite condition.
scope: spire-bearing brachiopods (Spiriferida, Atrypida, Athyridida and others)

label: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone
claim: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.
quote: In short, I think there is reason to believe, or at least to suspect, that we have in the shell and Aptychus of the Ammonites, two portions of a once united structure; of which other Cephalopods retain not both parts but only one or other, one as the ventrally situated shell of Nautilus, the other as the dorsally placed shell for example of Sepia or of Spirula.
scope: ammonoids, Nautilus, Sepia, Spirula and other cephalopods; thecosome pteropods

label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films
claim: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.
quote: In all cases, provided only that the membrane be isotropic, the form assumed will be precisely that of a soap-bubble under similar conditions of attachment: that is to say, it will be (with the usual limitations or conditions) a surface of minimal area.
scope: septa of nautiloid, orthocone and ammonoid shells

label: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon
claim: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.
quote: Superposed upon the usual sinuous outline, with its “lobes” and “saddles,” we have here a minutely ramified, or arborescent outline, in which all the branches terminate in wavy, more or less circular arcs,—looking just like the ‘landscape marble’ from the Bristol Rhaetic. We have no difficulty in recognising in this a surface-tension phenomenon.
scope: ammonoids with complex (ammonitic) suture lines

label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas
claim: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.
quote: Again, we find the same forms, or forms which (save for external ornament) are mathematically identical, repeating themselves in all periods of the world’s geological history; and, irrespective of climate or local conditions, we see them mixed up, one with another, in the depths and on the shores of every sea.
scope: spiral shells of molluscs, foraminifera and tube-dwelling worms through geological time

label: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms
claim: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.
quote: It is hard indeed (to my mind) to see where Natural Selection necessarily enters in, or to admit that it has had any share whatsoever in the production of these varied conformations.
scope: spiral shells of molluscs, foraminifera and worms
